chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), regarding a man who sold goods to another man, so the buyer took possession of the goods but did not pay the price, then the buyer died while the goods were still in their original state.
He said: 'If the goods are still in their original state, they are returned to the owner of the goods.' And he said: 'The creditors do not have the right to seize them (to satisfy their debts).'

key_terms.قَائِمٌ بِعَيْنِهِ: still in its original state / intact and identifiable

ai.seo_question: What happens to sold goods if the buyer dies before paying, and do creditors have a claim on them?
ai.summary: This ruling from the *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the priority of the seller's right to reclaim specific goods over general creditors, reflecting the Shia juristic principle that the item remains the seller's property until full payment is secured. It distinguishes this specific claim from the general estate distribution, ensuring the seller is not disadvantaged by the buyer's other liabilities. This mechanism underscores the importance of asset specificity in commercial transactions within Islamic inheritance law.
